hypotheses.hypothesis: Employ a pulse-modulated laser instead of a continuous wave laser during DED processing of AlCrFeNiSi to reduce the instantaneous peak temperature and thermal gradients.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock processed by conventional DED with continuous wave laser.
hypotheses.intervention: Replace the continuous wave laser with a pulse-modulated laser system having controlled on/off cycles.
hypotheses.conditions: DED processing under similar overall energy input conditions; laser pulse frequency and duty cycle to be optimized so that the average power remains similar while introducing off times at microsecond-to-millisecond scale.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Reduced melt pool peak temperatures and more uniform thermal gradients.
hypotheses.mechanism: Pulsing the laser allows transient cooling periods between pulses, which reduces the steepness of temperature gradients. This facilitates stress relaxation in the deposited layers and minimizes hot-spot-induced segregation or local compositional inhomogeneities. Reduced peak temperatures also limit rapid solidification defects. This mechanism builds on findings that lower peak temperatures (achieved by reducing laser power or extending dwell time) lead to reduced residual stresses (PMC10971808::web::005 and ::web::009).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A lower overall residual stress level and finer, more uniform microstructure with reduced segregation and defect formation compared to conventional continuous wave processing, with the mechanical integrity improved moderately (directionally improved; exact magnitude uncertain).
hypotheses.baseline: Conventional continuous wave DED processing of AlCrFeNiSi exhibits higher peak temperatures, steeper thermal gradients, and associated residual stresses as reported in similar Inconel studies.
hypotheses.boundary: Valid for DED processes where the pulse duration and off-time can be controlled without degrading process stability; may not work if pulse modulation results in insufficient melt pool stability.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Exact quantification of residual stress reduction is uncertain until experimentally optimized; the pulse parameters must be carefully balanced to avoid under-melting or excessive cooling.

hypotheses.what_is_new: Introducing pulse-modulated laser operation during DED for AlCrFeNiSi to transiently control thermal gradients, rather than merely modifying static parameters like laser power or dwell times.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Utilize a top‐hat laser beam profile for DED processing of AlCrFeNiSi to achieve a more uniform melt pool, thereby reducing thermal gradients that drive segregation and residual stress formation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock processed via standard DED with a Gaussian laser intensity profile.
hypotheses.intervention: Modify the laser optics to produce a top‐hat (uniform intensity) beam profile during deposition.
hypotheses.conditions: DED processing under standard conditions except for the beam homogenizer; applicable when the top‐hat profile can be maintained over the required focal depth.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: More uniform thermal distribution across the melt pool.
hypotheses.mechanism: A top‐hat profile provides a uniform intensity across the laser spot, leading to an even heat distribution in the created melt pool. This uniformity minimizes local hotspots and steep temperature gradients that promote compositional segregation and induce high residual stresses. The intervention leverages the concept that reducing temperature gradients (similar to using longer dwell times or lower laser power) leads to less residual stress (PMC10971808::web::009, PMC10971808::web::011).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A directional decrease in both residual stresses and segregation tendencies with improved mechanical integrity relative to the conventional Gaussian profile, although exact improvement values remain to be quantified.
hypotheses.baseline: Conventional DED with a Gaussian laser beam exhibits steep temperature gradients and localized hotspots, contributing to higher residual stress and segregation in AlCrFeNiSi.
hypotheses.boundary: Effective when the optical system can reliably generate and maintain a top‐hat profile; limited by the maximum laser power available and the optics quality.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise degree of stress reduction and homogeneity improvement is uncertain until system-specific tests are conducted.

hypotheses.mechanism: The induced ultrasonic vibrations create micro-agitations within the melt pool, promoting better mixing to counteract elemental segregation. paper_did: Developed a coupled thermo‐mechanical finite element model using ABAQUS 2019 to simulate directed energy deposition (DED) of Inconel 690 alloy.

Investigated the effect of key process parameters (laser power, scanning speed, substrate preheating temperature, and interlayer dwell time) on the temperature history and residual stress distribution during multi‐layer deposition.
Employed a Goldak double ellipsoid heat source model and progressive element activation to simulate the melt pool formation and layer-by-layer deposition on an Inconel 690 substrate.
paper_reported: The peak temperature of each deposited layer increases with higher laser power and preheating temperature and decreases with increased scanning speed and interlayer dwell time, with substrate preheating having a significant effect mainly on the first four layers.

Residual stresses were found to concentrate in the upper/middle region of the deposit, at the bottom of the substrate, and along the bonding interface; the stress magnitude increases with laser power and decreases with longer interlayer dwell times, while scanning speed and preheating temperature minimally affect residual stresses.
The simulation results correlate well with experimental temperature measurements and literature reports on stress distributions.
paper_proposed: Future studies could extend the finite element modeling to explore different scanning strategies and complex component geometries to predict residual stresses and strains more accurately, thereby aiding in the design of engineering components.

hypotheses.mechanism: Elevated build plate temperature lowers the cooling rate and temperature gradient, which reduces the magnitude of residual stresses and limits the formation of microstructural defects (such as vertical cracks). In addition, slower solidification helps avoid non-equilibrium segregation of elements at the melt pool boundaries, leading to improved phase distribution and mechanical integrity.

hypotheses.boundary: Valid for sample geometries and process parameters similar to current PBF-LB experiments; may be less effective for very large parts or when too high of a preheat temperature leads to other issues (e.g., excessive grain growth).
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimal preheating temperature and its influence on microstructure might require fine tuning; quantitative improvements are predicted directionally but not precisely quantified.

hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes the integration of a deliberate, controlled in-situ re-melting pass to simulate an annealing-like effect immediately post-layer formation, a processing strategy not explored in the paper for AlCrFeNiSi.

paper_did: Fabricated CrFeNiTi MPEA samples using two processing routes: laser powder‐bed fusion (PBF-LB) with a parameter study (varying laser power and scan speed corresponding to VED values from 50 to 100 J/mm³) and solid‐state sintering by HIP as a benchmark.

Prepared the MPEA feedstock via mechanical alloying of elemental and pre‐alloyed powders (L718 and W722) and characterized the resulting samples by optical microscopy, SEM, EDS (including line scans across the transition zone), micro‐hardness testing, and Thermocalc phase predictions.
paper_reported: PBF-LB samples produced with VED between 50 and 83 J/mm³ exhibited large, defect-free sections and an average micro‐hardness of about 965 HV0.1, whereas at the highest VED (100 J/mm³) a significant evaporation loss of Ti led to a ~30% drop in hardness.

A clear correlation was observed between local chemical composition (notably Ti content affecting the fraction of the C14 Laves phase) and mechanical properties, with distinct transition zones between the remelted substrate and the deposited material, and differences in microstructure (e.g., a finer top layer due to lack of subsequent reheating).
paper_proposed: Although not explicitly laid out as future work, the study alludes to processing improvements – such as the desirability of pre-alloyed powder, better control of thermal gradients (for example via build chamber preheating) and process modifications that could yield larger, defect‐free samples – that could help extend the findings.
